sentences.text: Paleontologist Matthew Bonnan found the remains in 2004 at a quarry on the Spion Kop 932 farm in the Free State region of South Africa.
A research team led by Blair W. McPhee and Matthew F. Bonnan officially named the genus and its type species Pulanesaura eocollum in 2015.
Scientists have examined partial skeletons belonging to at least two individuals, ranging from subadult to adult stages.
The main specimen, cataloged as BP/1/6982, is a front dorsal vertebra that is missing the tip of its neural spine.
Additional bones found nearby include teeth, ribs, a clavicle, limb elements, and claws.
Its skeletal structure indicates it was a low browser, eating plants near the ground unlike other prosauropods in the area.
A flexible neck allowed this animal to feed efficiently with very little movement of its body.
Unlike the prosauropods sharing its habitat, Pulanesaura fed at a lower level.
Research by Blair McPhee and colleagues suggests it coexisted with other sauropodomorphs by using different ecological niches.
Studies propose that this flexible neck helped conserve energy by reducing the need to move the body frequently while eating.
Pulanesaura is classified as a medium-sized transitional sauropodiform.
It belongs to the parent group Sauropoda.
The animal is placed within the class Saurischia.
This creature lived during the Early Jurassic, spanning from the late Hettangian to the Sinemurian stages in what is now South Africa.
It inhabited an arid floodplain where vegetation grew near river channels, allowing it to live alongside other sauropodomorphs like Aardonyx and Arcusaurus.
Its time range covers the Hettangian to the Sinemurian, between 201.4 and 192.9 million years ago.
Experts disagree on whether Pulanesaura is one of the least derived sauropods or the sister taxon to Sauropoda, depending on whether a node-based or stem-based definition of Sauropoda is used.
